categoryName: Not yet on the M1 schedule

questions.stem: A physiology researcher is tracing the sequence of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis that ends in cortisol synthesis. Which of the following hormones is secreted by the hypothalamus to initiate this cascade?

explanation.summary: The HPA axis begins with hypothalamic CRH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which activates the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then secretes ACTH, which triggers cortisol synthesis in the adrenal gland.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACTH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the hypothalamus, and acts downstream of CRH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid made in the adrenal gland and is not part of the CRH-ACTH-cortisol cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ADH regulates water balance and is not the hormone that initiates cortisol synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol is the end product synthesized in the adrenal gland, not the initiating hypothalamic signal.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on a corticosteroid, which markedly reduces joint inflammation. Which of the following best describes how corticosteroids decrease inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They decrease production of anti-inflammatory mediators such as IL-10 and IL-4

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase production of proinflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha and IL-2

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators equally

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit proinflammatory mediators and stimulate anti-inflammatory mediators

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators equally

explanation.summary: Cortisol shifts the balance away from inflammation on both sides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol inhibits production of proinflammatory mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, IL-2, IFN-gamma, IFN-alpha, TNF-alpha) while increasing anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, IL-4, IL-13). This dual action reduces the overall inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They increase anti-inflammatory mediators rather than decreasing them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids suppress, not increase, proinflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They do not inhibit anti-inflammatory mediators; those are increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They suppress proinflammatory mediators rather than stimulating them.

questions.stem: A pediatrician wants a single-dose corticosteroid for an asthma exacerbation that has high glucocorticoid activity and a long duration of action so it can be dosed once and exert its effect for several days. Which of the following corticosteroids best fits this profile?

explanation.summary: Dexamethasone has the highest glucocorticoid activity and a long duration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dexamethasone has a relative glucocorticoid activity of 30 and a long duration of action, making it well suited for single-dose use in a pediatric asthma exacerbation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisone has glucocorticoid activity of 1 and a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fludrocortisone is used exclusively as a mineralocorticoid and has essentially no glucocorticoid activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrocortisone has glucocorticoid activity of 1 and a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prednisone has moderate glucocorticoid activity (4) but only an intermediate duration.

questions.stem: A physician is deciding whether corticosteroids are safe in several patients. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to corticosteroid therapy because these drugs would worsen it directly?

explanation.summary: Immunosuppression makes an untreated systemic fungal infection an absolute contraindication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids suppress the immune system, leaving the body unable to fight a systemic fungal infection, so this is an absolute contraindication to their use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diabetes can be worsened by corticosteroids, but it is a relative caution rather than an absolute contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glaucoma can be aggravated by steroids but is not an absolute contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoporosis is worsened by steroids and warrants caution but is not the absolute contraindication tested here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncontrolled hypertension warrants caution but is not an absolute contraindication.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with persistent asthma needs long-term corticosteroid therapy, and the clinician wants to minimize systemic adverse effects. Which of the following strategies best reduces the systemic effects of corticosteroids in asthma treatment?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lowest effective dose for the shortest time

explanation.summary: Inhaled delivery keeps the drug in the airways and limits systemic absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids act mainly in the lungs and are minimally absorbed systemically, so they reduce systemic adverse effects while treating airway inflammation in asthma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Every-other-day dosing can lessen adrenal suppression but does not specifically limit systemic exposure the way inhaled delivery does.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intra-articular injections treat joints and are not a route used for asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Using the lowest effective dose is a general principle but does not target the airways or minimize systemic absorption as directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systemic corticosteroids actually increase systemic exposure and adverse effects.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on chronic high-dose oral steroids for temporal arteritis develops new-onset hyperglycemia requiring treatment. Drugs from which of the following classes are the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes mellitus?

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids are the leading cause of drug-induced diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids mimic cortisol, increasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and decreasing pancreatic insulin synthesis, which can cause new or worsen existing diabetes. This makes them the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes mellitus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics are not a leading cause of drug-induced diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antihistamines are not a significant cause of hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-blockers may blunt glucose recovery but are not the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NSAIDs are associated mainly with gastrointestinal adverse effects, not drug-induced diabetes.

questions.stem: Cortisol circulates at roughly 100 times the concentration of aldosterone and binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with similar affinity, yet aldosterone dominates mineralocorticoid signaling in the kidney. Which of the following best explains why cortisol does not overwhelm the mineralocorticoid receptor in these tissues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol to cortisone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldosterone has a 100-fold higher affinity for the receptor than cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol is entirely bound to plasma proteins and cannot enter cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cortisol is unable to bind the mineralocorticoid receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid receptors are located only in the central nervous system

explanation.summary: An enzyme protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol.
explanation.whyCorrect: In mineralocorticoid target tissues, 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol into inactive cortisone. This 'protects' the mineralocorticoid receptor so aldosterone, rather than the far more abundant cortisol, dominates its signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The two hormones have similar receptor affinity; aldosterone does not simply out-compete cortisol by affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol is not fully protein-bound; free cortisol readily enters cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol does bind the mineralocorticoid receptor with affinity similar to aldosterone; that is exactly the problem the enzyme solves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mineralocorticoid receptors are present in the kidney, colon, and salivary and sweat glands, not only the CNS.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents in preterm labor at 30 weeks of gestation. To accelerate fetal lung maturity and reduce neonatal respiratory complications, the obstetrician administers an intramuscular corticosteroid. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Antenatal betamethasone accelerates fetal lung development.
explanation.whyCorrect: Betamethasone given intramuscularly (12 mg, two doses 24 hours apart) for preterm labor accelerates development of type I and type II pneumocytes, improving lung mechanics and surfactant production and reducing neonatal morbidity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisone is a short-acting agent with low glucocorticoid potency and is not the antenatal agent used for lung maturity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for salt retention, not fetal lung maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, not a corticosteroid used to mature fetal lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical hydrocortisone treats skin conditions and would not reach the fetus systemically.

questions.stem: A patient is given a mineralocorticoid, which acts on the principal cells of the renal collecting duct. Which of the following best describes the net effect of aldosterone at this site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased reabsorption of both sodium and potassium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased free water excretion with no change in sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased sodium excretion and increased potassium reabsorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased sodium reabsorption and increased potassium excretion

explanation.summary: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and wastes potassium in the collecting duct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption by upregulating luminal sodium channels and the Na+/K+-ATPase pump. The pump drives potassium into the cell, and increased potassium channels then secrete it into the urine, so the net effect is sodium reabsorption with potassium excretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption rather than decreasing transport of both ions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone acts on sodium and potassium handling, not calcium and phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium reabsorption drives concurrent water reabsorption, expanding plasma volume, not free water excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and excretes potassium, the opposite of this choice.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who has taken high-dose prednisone for a year after a kidney transplant abruptly stops the medication. Over the next two days he develops fatigue, nausea, and profound hypotension. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

explanation.summary: Abrupt steroid withdrawal after chronic use precipitates adrenal crisis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged exogenous corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis, leading to adrenal suppression and inadequate endogenous cortisol production. Sudden discontinuation unmasks adrenal insufficiency, which is why corticosteroids are tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anaphylaxis occurs on exposure to a drug, not on its discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cushing syndrome results from excess, not deficient, corticosteroid effect and would not follow abrupt withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia, not hypotension after steroid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steroids raise blood glucose while being taken; stopping them would not cause hypotension and these symptoms.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been taking prednisone and recently added regular ibuprofen for joint pain. She now presents with epigastric pain and melena. The concurrent use of these two drugs most notably increases her risk of which of the following adverse effects?

explanation.summary: Steroids plus NSAIDs sharply raise the risk of ulcers and GI bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids increase gastric acid secretion and predispose to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. This risk increases nearly four-fold when they are combined with NSAIDs, which fits this patient's epigastric pain and melena.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal suppression relates to prolonged systemic steroid exposure, not to NSAID co-administration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glaucoma is a steroid effect on the eye and is unrelated to combining steroids with NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral thrush is linked to inhaled corticosteroids, not to the steroid-NSAID combination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoporosis is a long-term steroid effect but is not specifically potentiated by adding an NSAID.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy using an inhaled corticosteroid daily for asthma develops white, curd-like plaques on his tongue and buccal mucosa that scrape off to reveal an erythematous base. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Inhaled steroids predispose to oral Candida infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce the local immune response in the mouth and throat, allowing opportunistic Candida albicans to cause oral thrush, which presents as removable white plaques. Rinsing the mouth after each inhaler use helps prevent it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aphthous ulcers are shallow painful ulcers, not white curd-like plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpetic stomatitis produces painful vesicles and ulcers, not scrapable white plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukoplakia forms adherent white patches that do not scrape off and is not caused by inhaled steroids in a child.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lichen planus produces lacy white striae that are fixed, not removable plaques from steroid use.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis takes an over-the-counter H1 antihistamine and notices that her runny nose improves. This symptom relief is most directly explained by which of the following actions of the drug on endothelial cells adjacent to vascular smooth muscle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of mast cell degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of nitric oxide and prostacyclin release

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines reduce nasal symptoms by blocking H1 receptors, which inhibits nitric oxide and prostacyclin release and produces vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: By antagonizing H1 receptors on endothelial cells, the drug inhibits the release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin. This causes vasoconstriction and reduces edema formation, lessening runny nose symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H1 antihistamines act on histamine receptors, not nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking gastric acid secretion is a function of H2 blockers, not H1 antihistamines used for allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor; they do not trigger mast cell degranulation, which is what releases histamine in the first place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased nitric oxide and prostacyclin would cause vasodilation and worsen edema, the opposite of the drug's effect.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man takes diphenhydramine for allergies and becomes very drowsy, while his coworker taking loratadine for the same allergies reports no sedation. Which property of diphenhydramine best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is hydrophilic and cannot enter the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: It selectively blocks H2 receptors in the stomach

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier, blocking central H1 receptors and causing sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines are lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so they block central H1 receptors that normally promote wakefulness, producing drowsiness. Second-generation drugs like loratadine are hydrophilic and penetrate the brain poorly, so they are non-sedating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation, not a second-generation, antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is lipophilic, not hydrophilic; that is precisely why it enters the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diphenhydramine blocks H1, not H2 receptors, and H2 blockade would not explain sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug blocks H1 receptors; it does not stimulate central histamine release.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a non-sedating antihistamine for chronic urticaria so that daytime alertness is preserved. Which of the following agents best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine are non-sedating because they poorly cross the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine. These agents are hydrophilic, act primarily on peripheral H1 receptors, and cause little sedation, making them ideal when alertness must be preserved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation agent that crosses the blood-brain barrier and can cause sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is a lipophilic first-generation agent that causes marked drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine and is sedating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is a first-generation agent with sedating and antimuscarinic properties.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is brought in for confusion, blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty urinating that began after he started an over-the-counter first-generation antihistamine. These findings are best explained by the drug's action at which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Many first-generation antihistamines also block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines have antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) activity. Blockade of muscarinic receptors causes dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and, especially in the elderly, confusion and delirium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2 blockade relates to bronchial and vascular tone, not dry mouth and urinary retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal effects, not the dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 receptors regulate gastric acid; blocking them does not cause this anticholinergic toxidrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic receptor blockade would affect the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, not this pattern of anticholinergic findings.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has persistent nausea and vomiting. Her physician prescribes doxylamine in combination with which of the following, an FDA-approved regimen for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?

explanation.summary: Doxylamine plus vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is an approved treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that doxylamine, a first-generation antihistamine, combined with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), is approved for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. First-generation agents cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects but is not the antiemetic partner of doxylamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 is used for pernicious anemia, not paired with doxylamine for pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C is not part of this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D addresses bone and calcium metabolism, not nausea of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A family planning a road trip asks for a medication to prevent motion sickness in an adult. Which antihistamine is most appropriate, and what property makes it effective for this indication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cetirizine, because it is hydrophilic and non-sedating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desloratadine, because it blocks H2 receptors in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fexofenadine, because it acts only at peripheral sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loratadine, because it is non-sedating and long acting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promethazine, because of its antimuscarinic properties

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines with antimuscarinic activity, such as promethazine, are effective against motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that first-generation antihistamines like promethazine and dimenhydrinate have antimuscarinic properties that make them effective in treating motion sickness. Second-generation agents lack this activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cetirizine is a second-generation agent lacking meaningful antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desloratadine is an H1, not H2, agent and is second-generation; it is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fexofenadine acts only peripherally and is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loratadine is a peripherally acting second-generation agent without the antimuscarinic activity needed for motion sickness.

questions.stem: In a review of histamine physiology, a student notes where the H1 receptor is located relative to other histamine receptor subtypes. According to the brick, where are H2 histamine receptors primarily located?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems

explanation.summary: H2 histamine receptors are found primarily in gastric cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that H2 histamine receptors are primarily in gastric cells, H3 receptors in the neurons, and H4 receptors in the bone marrow, whereas H1 receptors are widespread and are the target of antihistamine therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bone marrow is the location of H4, not H2, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neurons are where H3 receptors are located.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vascular endothelial cells express the H1 receptors targeted by antihistamines, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Widespread distribution in the central and peripheral nervous systems describes H1 receptors.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is given a first-generation antihistamine and, instead of becoming sleepy, develops restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia. This response is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sign of H2 receptor blockade

choices.label: C
choices.text: A withdrawal effect from stopping the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: An allergic reaction to the drug

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines can cause paradoxical CNS stimulation in children younger than about six years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick warns that in children younger than six, first-generation antihistamines can, at regular doses, cause a paradoxical CNS stimulation manifesting as restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia rather than the usual drowsiness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These first-generation agents act at H1 and muscarinic receptors, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reaction occurred after taking the drug, not after stopping it, so it is not withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The symptoms are a CNS drug effect, not an allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The child is stimulated, not sedated, so this is not the expected sedative effect.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine for seasonal allergies. Through its anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) action, this drug is most likely to produce which of the following effects in the eye?

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinic action at the eye causes pupil dilation and reduced tear formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 lists the ocular anticholinergic effects as mydriasis (dilation) and decreased lacrimation, which clinically produce blurred vision and dry eyes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimuscarinic effects decrease, not increase, intestinal motility, causing constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antimuscarinic activity decreases sweating rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antimuscarinic activity decreases urination, causing retention, not increased output.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Miosis and increased tears are cholinergic effects, the opposite of antimuscarinic blockade.

questions.stem: A patient taking a second-generation antihistamine for allergies reports only a mild headache and occasional fatigue, with no significant dry mouth or drowsiness. This favorable side-effect profile compared with first-generation agents is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced release of histamine from mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greater lipophilicity and stronger blood-brain barrier penetration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible binding to H1 receptors in the brain

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines penetrate the brain poorly and have little antimuscarinic activity, so side effects are mild and non-specific.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because second-generation agents are hydrophilic and act mainly on peripheral H1 receptors, they cause much less sedation and few antimuscarinic effects. Their adverse effects are usually mild and non-specific, such as headache, diarrhea, or fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor and do not enhance histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Greater lipophilicity and brain penetration would increase, not decrease, sedation, and describes first-generation agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 antihistamines are competitive (reversible) H1 blockers, not irreversible binders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These drugs block H1 receptors; nicotinic blockade is not their mechanism.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man reports several weeks of new daytime sleepiness. Medication review reveals he recently added an over-the-counter pill containing diphenhydramine to help him sleep. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to address his sleepiness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a second-generation antihistamine on top of the diphenhydramine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add an H2 blocker to counteract the sedation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to promethazine for its antimuscarinic effect

explanation.summary: Sedation from a first-generation antihistamine is managed by stopping the offending drug and substituting a non-sedating agent if needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case, the patient's new sleepiness is caused by diphenhydramine, a sedating first-generation antihistamine. The remedy is to stop that drug and, if antihistamine therapy is still needed, replace it with a non-sedating second-generation agent such as loratadine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding another antihistamine keeps the sedating diphenhydramine on board and does not fix the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An H2 blocker treats gastric acid and would not counteract the sedation from an H1 agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing the dose of the sedating drug would worsen the sleepiness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is another sedating first-generation agent and would not relieve the drowsiness.

questions.stem: H1 antihistamines are best classified pharmacologically as which of the following with respect to the H1 receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive antagonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full agonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective agonists at H2 and H3 receptors

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines act by competitively binding to H1 receptors as antagonists or inverse agonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes H1 antihistamines as histamine antagonists and inverse agonists that work by competitively binding to H1 receptors, thereby blocking histamine's effects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: They are receptor blockers, not enzymes that degrade histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They oppose, rather than activate, the H1 receptor, so they are not full agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They block the receptor; they do not inhibit histamine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They target the H1 receptor and are not agonists at H2 or H3 receptors.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has taken oxycodone for chronic back pain for several months. Initially his pain was well controlled, but he now reports that the same dose no longer relieves it and he requires progressively higher amounts. Which of the following cellular changes best explains this loss of effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desensitization and downregulation of opioid receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of neutralizing antibodies against oxycodone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of hepatic CYP enzymes producing an inactive metabolite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible mutation of the opioid receptor gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of opioid receptors on target neurons

explanation.summary: Tolerance reflects desensitization and downregulation of opioid receptors after chronic agonist exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: With frequent opioid agonist use, opioid receptors become desensitized and downregulated, reducing signaling across all pathways so that higher doses are needed to produce the same effect. This tolerance can begin as early as two weeks of consistent use.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioids do not act by triggering neutralizing antibodies; tolerance is receptor-based.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes tolerance to receptor changes, not to accelerated hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tolerance is a reversible adaptive change, not an irreversible genetic mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic agonist exposure downregulates rather than upregulates opioid receptors.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman abruptly stops taking the opioids she has used daily for months. Within a day she develops tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils, shakiness, muscle pain, and severe anxiety. Activation of which of the following brainstem structures is most responsible for these findings?

explanation.summary: Opioid withdrawal is driven physiologically by activation of the locus coeruleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Withdrawal is the body's response to abruptly stopping the drug. Its physiological basis is complex but involves activation of the locus coeruleus in the pons of the brainstem, a region normally involved in stress and panic responses, producing autonomic symptoms such as tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated pupils.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The nucleus accumbens participates in reward, but the brick names the locus coeruleus for withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The substantia nigra governs motor control and dopamine in Parkinson disease, not opioid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythm, not withdrawal physiology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ventral tegmental area is a reward/dopamine center, not the driver of withdrawal symptoms here.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is found unresponsive on the sidewalk. He has pinpoint pupils, a respiratory rate of 4/min with shallow breathing, and cyanotic lips. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic treatment?

explanation.summary: Naloxone is the reversal agent for opioid overdose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The findings are classic opioid overdose. Naloxone is a full opioid antagonist that binds and inhibits opioid receptors, displacing the agonist and reversing respiratory depression, which is the life-threatening feature here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist used to ease withdrawal during discontinuation, not to reverse an acute overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Docusate is a stool softener for opioid-induced constipation and has no role in overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methadone is a long-acting agonist for maintenance therapy and would worsen respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a heroin overdose is given naloxone in the emergency department and rapidly improves. About 45 minutes later she again becomes somnolent with slow, shallow breathing. Which of the following best explains this recurrence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Naloxone accumulated in the liver and released the opioid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Naloxone caused rebound upregulation of opioid receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than the opioid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Naloxone is a partial agonist that wears off into agonist activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient rapidly developed tolerance to naloxone

explanation.summary: Naloxone's duration of action is shorter than that of many opioids, so effects can return.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the duration of action of the opioid antagonist is shorter than that of the agonists, so repeat doses of naloxone are often required in overdose situations. As naloxone wears off while opioid still occupies receptors, respiratory depression can recur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naloxone does not sequester and later release the opioid from the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recurrence is due to naloxone's short duration, not receptor upregulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Naloxone is a full antagonist, not a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance to naloxone over 45 minutes is not the mechanism described in the brick.

questions.stem: A first responder administers a medication that competitively displaces an opioid already bound to its receptors and has no agonist activity of its own. Which of the following best describes this drug's mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of the benzodiazepine binding site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full antagonism of all three opioid receptor types

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of the CYP enzymes that metabolize the opioid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Partial agonism at the mu opioid receptor

explanation.summary: Naloxone is a full opioid antagonist that binds all three receptor types.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike full or partial agonists, opioid antagonists fully bind and inhibit opioid receptors and can displace an agonist that is already bound. Naloxone, the classic example, antagonizes all three opioid receptor types and reverses respiratory depression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the benzodiazepine site describes flumazenil, not an opioid antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioid antagonists act at opioid receptors, not by enhancing GABA signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug acts at the receptor, not by inhibiting hepatic metabolism of the opioid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Partial agonism describes buprenorphine, not the full antagonist being described.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with opioid use disorder is about to be started on methadone for maintenance therapy. Which of the following studies should be obtained before initiating this medication, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fasting glucose, because methadone causes hyperglycemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: An ECG, because methadone can prolong the QTc

choices.label: C
choices.text: An MRI of the brain, because methadone raises intracranial pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liver function tests, because methadone is directly hepatotoxic

explanation.summary: Methadone prolongs the QTc, so an ECG is obtained before starting it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methadone influences cardiac muscle and can prolong the QTc, the interval between Q-wave polarization and T-wave repolarization. A prolonged QTc can lead to ventricular arrhythmias, so an ECG must be performed before a patient starts methadone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperglycemia is not the concern that prompts baseline testing before methadone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methadone is not associated with raised intracranial pressure requiring an MRI.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick highlights QTc prolongation as the reason for pre-treatment testing, not direct hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methadone's lethal cardiac effect is QTc prolongation, not bronchoconstriction detected by spirometry.

questions.stem: A patient with an opioid overdose has progressively slow, shallow breathing that leads to a rising arterial pCO2 and eventual respiratory arrest. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the respiratory depression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A large increase in metabolic CO2 production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct paralysis of the diaphragm muscle fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary edema from acute fluid overload

explanation.summary: Opioids reduce respiratory drive by lowering the brainstem's chemosensitivity to CO2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioids reduce respiratory drive by binding mu receptors. Their inhibitory effects decrease the brain's chemosensitivity to high blood pCO2 and to hypoxia, so breathing slows and becomes shallow; ventilation falls, arterial pCO2 rises, and the result can be unconsciousness, respiratory arrest, and death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The problem is decreased ventilation, not increased CO2 production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism is reduced central drive, not airway bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opioids depress the central respiratory drive rather than directly paralyzing diaphragm fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory failure here is from hypoventilation, not fluid-overload pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman is being started on a scheduled opioid for chronic pain. To prevent a common and predictable adverse effect, which of the following is most appropriate to prescribe alongside the opioid?

explanation.summary: Opioid-induced constipation is anticipated and prevented with a stool softener or laxative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioids reduce bowel motility, and opioid-induced constipation is a common, concerning adverse effect. It is common practice to prescribe a stool softener such as docusate, or a laxative, even before the patient has symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An antiemetic may help nausea but does not address the predictable constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Raising the opioid dose worsens, rather than prevents, gastrointestinal adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loperamide is an antidiarrheal that slows the gut further and would worsen constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Naloxone reverses overdose and would precipitate withdrawal, not prevent constipation.

questions.stem: A physician is distinguishing dependence from addiction in a patient on chronic opioids. Which of the following statements best describes addiction as defined in the brick?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A physiologic adaptation requiring the drug to feel normal at baseline

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autonomic symptoms that appear after abruptly stopping the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences

choices.label: D
choices.text: Needing progressively higher doses to achieve the same effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversal of the drug's effect when an antagonist is administered

explanation.summary: Addiction is a chronic relapsing brain disease of compulsive use despite harm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the National Institute on Drug Abuse definition cited in the brick, addiction is a chronic, relapsing brain disease characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences. This is distinct from dependence, which is a physiologic adaptation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Requiring the drug to function at baseline describes dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autonomic symptoms after abrupt cessation describe withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Needing higher doses for the same effect describes tolerance, not addiction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversal of effect by an antagonist describes the action of naloxone, not addiction.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man on long-term opioids for chronic pain wishes to discontinue them while minimizing severe withdrawal. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic strategy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double the opioid dose and then stop

explanation.summary: A partial agonist such as buprenorphine helps mitigate withdrawal during discontinuation.
explanation.whyCorrect: To limit withdrawal symptoms in patients discontinuing opioids, a tapering strategy or the partial agonist buprenorphine may be used. Buprenorphine partially activates opioid receptors, blunting withdrawal as the patient comes off opioids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naloxone is a full antagonist that would precipitate acute withdrawal in a dependent patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing the dose worsens dependence rather than easing discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in opioid discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abrupt cessation produces the severe withdrawal the plan is meant to avoid.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects heroin presents with fever, a new heart murmur, and blood cultures positive for bacteria. This complication is most directly related to which of the following?

explanation.summary: Needle sharing during IV opioid use causes bloodborne infections such as endocarditis and sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary adverse effects from opioid abuse include infections when opioids are used intravenously outside the medical system. Needle sharing exposes users to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections and can cause heart valve infections or systemic bacterial infection (sepsis), which can be fatal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Withdrawal produces autonomic symptoms, not a bacteremic valvular infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tolerance is a receptor adaptation and does not cause bloodborne infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: QTc prolongation is a methadone cardiac effect, not a cause of infective endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Constipation is a gastrointestinal effect unrelated to endocarditis.

questions.stem: An opioid-dependent patient is given naloxone in the emergency department. Minutes later he becomes agitated and diaphoretic with tachycardia and dilated pupils. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An anaphylactic allergic reaction to naloxone

explanation.summary: Because naloxone blocks all opioid receptors, it can precipitate immediate withdrawal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that because naloxone antagonizes all opioid receptors after administration, it can cause immediate withdrawal, and patients may be violent and agitated following its use. The agitation, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and dilated pupils are classic withdrawal findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The signs are the autonomic picture of withdrawal, not urticaria and airway compromise of anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The patient received naloxone, not methadone, and shows withdrawal rather than sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no serotonergic agent described, and the picture matches opioid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Naloxone reverses opioid effects; it does not deepen the overdose.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is started on an opioid for severe postoperative pain. His physician explains that although the drug binds several opioid receptor subtypes, most of its pain-relieving effect comes from activation of one particular receptor. Activation of which of the following receptors is responsible for the majority of an opioid's analgesic effect?

explanation.summary: Most of the analgesic properties of opioids are mediated by the mu-opioid receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that most of the analgesic properties of opioids are due to activation of the mu-opioid receptor, including activation in the periaqueductal gray that blocks the sensation of pain. Mu, kappa, and delta are the three receptors involved in analgesia, but the mu receptor carries the bulk of the effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Delta-opioid receptors contribute to analgesia and modulate mu activity but are found in the fewest brain areas and mainly produce antidepressant/anxiolytic effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kappa-opioid receptors provide and modulate analgesia but are not targeted for long-term analgesia because they cause dysphoria and depression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Omega is not an opioid receptor type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sigma is not one of the three primary opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta) involved in analgesia.

questions.stem: A pharmacology instructor compares two opioids that both bind the mu-opioid receptor with high affinity. She notes that the full agonist produces a wider array of signaling cascades and a greater maximal physiologic effect than the partial agonist. The full agonist differs from the partial agonist primarily by having a higher which of the following?

explanation.summary: A full agonist has ~100% efficacy at the receptor, whereas a partial agonist has lower efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that full agonists completely bind receptors and produce the full array of physiologic effects, giving them higher efficacy than partial agonists. A full agonist has 100% efficacy when binding to a receptor, whereas a partial agonist produces a lesser (partial) effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absorption is a pharmacokinetic property that is not what distinguishes full from partial agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duration reflects how long the drug remains bound and acts, and is independent of full versus partial agonism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both full and partial agonists bind with high affinity; the difference lies in efficacy, not affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excretion is a pharmacokinetic property and is not the defining difference.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with acute severe pain from a long-bone fracture. The team wants an opioid route that avoids first-pass metabolism and provides the quickest onset of analgesia. Which of the following routes of administration best meets these goals?

explanation.summary: The intravenous route avoids first-pass metabolism and gives the fastest onset, making it preferred for acute severe pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies IV as the preferred route for acute severe pain because it provides a quicker onset of action, avoids first-pass metabolism, and most often yields higher bioavailability than the oral route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IM avoids first-pass metabolism but has a slower onset than IV and is the least common route for opioids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral opioids are subject to first-pass metabolism and have a slower onset and potentially lower bioavailability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rectal route is not described as the preferred rapid-onset route for acute severe pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transdermal delivery is slow-absorbing and used for chronic/sustained pain, not rapid onset.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man of Asian descent is given a standard analgesic dose of an opioid after surgery. He becomes excessively sedated and develops respiratory depression, and the effect of a single dose lasts far longer than expected. A CYP2D6 phenotype is suspected. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has enhanced renal clearance shortening the drug's half-life

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has induced CYP2D6 activity, lowering opioid levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a poor metabolizer, so clearance is slowed

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is an ultrarapid metabolizer, so the opioid is cleared very quickly

choices.label: E
choices.text: He lacks opioid receptors, increasing free drug in plasma

explanation.summary: Poor CYP2D6 metabolizers clear opioids slowly, prolonging drug action and risking overdose; this phenotype is most common in individuals of Asian descent (up to 35%).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that poor metabolizers have altered pharmacokinetics that prolong the duration of action, so a single dose can last two to three times as long as expected and cause unintended overdose. Poor metabolizers are most common among individuals of Asian descent (up to 35%).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes altered opioid duration to CYP2D6 hepatic metabolism, not to enhanced renal clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Induced CYP2D6 would lower opioid levels and reduce effect, the opposite of this prolonged toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ultrarapid metabolizers clear drug quickly and have shorter, not prolonged, durations of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opioid receptor number is not the mechanism of altered duration described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with opioid use disorder is started on a medication to help manage his condition. His physician selects a drug that binds the mu-opioid receptor with high affinity but only partially activates it, so that at high doses the patient gets less of a 'high.' Which of the following medications was most likely prescribed?

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is the most common partial mu-opioid agonist and is used in opioid use disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes buprenorphine as the most common partial agonist of the mu-opioid receptor. It binds with high affinity but only partially activates the receptor, so at high doses patients get less of a 'high,' making it useful in opioid use disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Codeine is a weak full agonist (and prodrug), not a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fentanyl is a strong full agonist and would not blunt the 'high' as described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydromorphone is a strong full agonist, not a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Morphine is a strong full agonist used as the potency benchmark, not a partial agonist.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is given codeine for pain after a tonsillectomy. Hours later he develops profound respiratory depression. Genetic testing reveals a CYP2D6 polymorphism. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codeine directly antagonizes brainstem mu receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codeine induces its own metabolism, raising active metabolite levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Poor CYP2D6 metabolism prevents codeine from being activated at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced renal excretion accumulates unchanged codeine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolism converts codeine to morphine

explanation.summary: Codeine is a prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to morphine; ultrarapid metabolizers generate toxic morphine levels, the basis of the FDA black box warning in children under 12.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that codeine has an FDA black box warning in children under 12 because codeine is metabolized by CYP2D6 into morphine; children who are ultrarapid metabolizers convert it rapidly, producing dangerously high morphine levels that cause severe respiratory depression and death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codeine is an agonist prodrug, not a brainstem mu-receptor antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism is genetic ultrarapid metabolism, not autoinduction by codeine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Poor metabolizers would produce too little morphine and inadequate analgesia, not respiratory depression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The toxicity is driven by CYP2D6 conversion to morphine, not by reduced renal excretion of codeine.

questions.stem: A researcher studies a kappa-opioid receptor agonist and observes that it produces a diuretic effect. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for this kappa-mediated diuresis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of aquaporin channels in the collecting duct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of renal tubular sodium reabsorption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased release of antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the release of oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone

explanation.summary: Kappa-opioid receptor activation causes diuresis by inhibiting release of oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that kappa receptors can cause a prominent diuretic effect by inhibiting the release of oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Less ADH means less water reabsorption and increased urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RAAS activation is not the mechanism described for kappa-mediated diuresis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes decreased ADH release, not direct aquaporin blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the diuresis to reduced ADH/oxytocin release, not direct tubular sodium handling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased ADH release would cause water retention (antidiuresis), the opposite of the observed effect.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with opioid use disorder needs a maintenance opioid that is a full agonist with an ultra-long duration of action to provide a sustained effect. Which of the following medications best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Methadone is a full agonist with an ultra-long duration, useful for sustained control in opioid use disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes methadone as a full agonist with an ultra-long duration of action, making it useful for a sustained effect in patients with opioid use disorder. It is listed as a strong, long-duration full agonist.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codeine is a weak, short-acting full agonist, not an ultra-long-acting maintenance agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Meperidine is a weak, short-acting full agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Morphine is a strong full agonist but has a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tramadol is a weak, short-acting full agonist.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with cancer-related chronic pain is managed with an opioid delivered by a skin patch that is absorbed slowly, provides stable blood levels, and extends the drug's duration of action even though the opioid itself is short-acting. Which of the following opioids is most commonly used in this way?

explanation.summary: Fentanyl transdermal patches are the most common transdermal opioid; slow skin absorption prolongs duration and gives stable levels for chronic/cancer pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that fentanyl transdermal patches are the most common transdermal opioids and are especially useful for cancer-related pain. Although fentanyl is short-acting, the slow rate of absorption through the skin increases its duration of action and provides stable blood levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist used mainly for opioid use disorder in this brick, not the described cancer-pain patch.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codeine is a weak oral antitussive/analgesic prodrug, not the transdermal patch opioid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meperidine is a weak short-acting full agonist and is not used as the transdermal agent described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Morphine is a strong short-acting full agonist but is not the opioid identified for transdermal patch use.

questions.stem: A medical student reviews how opioids initiate their intracellular signaling. Opioid receptors, including the mu, kappa, and delta subtypes, belong to which of the following receptor superfamilies?

explanation.summary: Opioid receptors are 7-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that opioid receptors are 7-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) with three primary types: mu, kappa, and delta.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nuclear receptors are intracellular transcription-factor receptors, unlike the membrane GPCR opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligand-gated ion channels (e.g., nicotinic, GABA-A) are a different superfamily from the GPCR opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor tyrosine kinases (e.g., insulin receptor) are not the class of opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Voltage-gated ion channels respond to membrane potential, not to opioid ligand binding as GPCRs do.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on chronic opioid therapy for arthritis pain develops persistent constipation that does not improve with continued use. Which of the following best explains this common opioid side effect?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kappa-receptor activation increases secretion from intestinal glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opioids block absorption of dietary fiber in the small intestine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opioids increase release of antidiuretic hormone, drying the stool

explanation.summary: Mu-opioid receptors on enteric neurons reliably decrease GI motility, producing constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mu-opioid receptors are densely distributed in the enteric neurons of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, and opioid agonists reliably decrease gastric motility, so patients commonly develop constipation and changes in bowel function. Unlike some effects, tolerance to constipation does not readily develop.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Opioids slow rather than stimulate peristalsis; delta receptors are linked to mood effects, not increased gut motility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes constipation to decreased motility via mu receptors, not increased kappa-mediated intestinal secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking fiber absorption is not the mechanism of opioid-induced constipation described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ADH release relates to kappa-mediated diuresis, not to the mechanism of opioid constipation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man brought in after an opioid overdose has a respiratory rate of 4 breaths per minute. His toxicity is due to opioid action at the mu-opioid receptor in the central respiratory centers. Which of the following best describes how opioids depress respiration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They cause bronchoconstriction that limits gas exchange

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase the ventilatory response to rising carbon dioxide

choices.label: C
choices.text: They paralyze the diaphragm by blocking neuromuscular junction receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: They reduce the intrinsic rhythm generators

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid body

explanation.summary: Opioids depress respiration by reducing the intrinsic rhythm generators in the ventrolateral medulla, slowing the breathing rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that opioid agonists depress respiratory activity by causing a reduction to the intrinsic rhythm generators located in the ventrolateral medulla, producing a slower rate of breathing; at toxic doses the respiratory rate may fall to 3-4 breaths per minute.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Respiratory depression here is central and rate-based, not due to bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioids blunt, rather than increase, the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioids act centrally on medullary respiratory centers, not by blocking the neuromuscular junction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opioids depress central respiratory rhythm rather than stimulating carotid body chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage 1 hypertension is started on lisinopril. The drug lowers his blood pressure by interfering with a specific step in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Which of the following steps does lisinopril inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of angiotensin II to its type 1 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of angiotensinogen into angiotensin I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion of angiotensin I into angiotensin II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of aldosterone directly from the adrenal cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of renin from juxtaglomerular cells

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, halting formation of angiotensin II.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE, found largely in the lungs, catalyzes conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By blocking this enzyme, ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II, decreasing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release and thereby lowering blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the angiotensin II type 1 receptor is the mechanism of ARBs (sartans), not ACE inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Renin, not ACE, cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin I; ACE inhibitors do not affect this step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone secretion falls indirectly because angiotensin II is reduced, not through direct blockade at the adrenal cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting renin release is the mechanism of renin inhibitors such as aliskiren.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman who developed a persistent dry cough on enalapril is switched to losartan, which controls her blood pressure without the cough. By what mechanism does losartan lower blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly relaxing arteriolar smooth muscle independent of angiotensin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibiting renin release from the kidney

explanation.summary: ARBs block the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, preventing angiotensin II from acting.
explanation.whyCorrect: ARBs such as losartan block angiotensin II at its type 1 receptor. Angiotensin II is still produced (ACE is not inhibited) but cannot exert vasoconstriction or promote aldosterone release. Because bradykinin metabolism is unaffected, ARBs have a much lower incidence of cough than ACE inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking aldosterone receptors describes spironolactone, not an ARB.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ARBs work through the angiotensin receptor, not by direct nonspecific arteriolar relaxation like a calcium channel blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting ACE is the mechanism of the -pril drugs; losartan is an ARB and does not block ACE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin inhibitors act one step earlier by blocking renin; ARBs act at the receptor.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman started on lisinopril three weeks ago presents with a dry, hacking cough that is worse at night. She has no fever, wheezing, or sputum production. Accumulation of which of the following substances most likely explains her cough?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor cough is caused by accumulation of bradykinin.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE normally degrades bradykinin. When ACE is inhibited, bradykinin accumulates; as a bronchoconstrictive inflammatory mediator it increases vascular permeability and causes bronchial smooth muscle contraction, producing a dry cough. Switching to an ARB, which does not affect bradykinin, usually relieves it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone is reduced by RAAS inhibition and is unrelated to the cough.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiotensin II levels fall with an ACE inhibitor and do not cause the cough.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histamine mediates allergic reactions but is not the ACE inhibitor cough mechanism described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potassium retention causes hyperkalemia, not cough.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with heart failure taking lisinopril and spironolactone is found on routine labs to have a serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L. Which mechanism best explains the hyperkalemia attributable to his ACE inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bradykinin-induced shift of potassium out of cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct blockade of renal potassium channels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased glomerular filtration promoting potassium loss

explanation.summary: RAAS inhibition lowers aldosterone, reducing renal potassium excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: By reducing angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex. Less aldosterone means less renal tubular secretion of potassium, leading to potassium retention and hyperkalemia. Risk is amplified by potassium-sparing agents such as spironolactone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bradykinin causes cough and angioedema, not a transcellular potassium shift here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ACE inhibitors act through aldosterone, not by directly blocking renal potassium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone is decreased, not increased, by an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ACE inhibitors tend to lower GFR, and this is not the mechanism of hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with dehydration from several days of gastroenteritis is started on ramipril for hypertension. Two days later her serum creatinine rises and her glomerular filtration rate falls. Which renal hemodynamic change best explains this acute decline in GFR?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physical obstruction of the renal tubule

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering GFR, especially in volume-depleted patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under normal conditions angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain glomerular pressure and GFR. ACE inhibitors and ARBs block this, dilating the efferent arteriole and reducing glomerular hydrostatic pressure, which acutely lowers GFR. This prerenal effect is pronounced with dehydration or heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Afferent constriction is not the mechanism; the brick attributes the GFR drop to loss of efferent tone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Efferent constriction is the normal angiotensin II effect that the drug blocks, not causes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure decreases, not increases, which is why GFR falls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is a prerenal hemodynamic effect, not a postrenal tubular obstruction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man maintained on lisinopril begins taking ibuprofen several times daily for arthritis pain. He subsequently develops acute kidney injury. Why does combining an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor increase this risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated dilation of the afferent arteriole

choices.label: B
choices.text: NSAIDs dilate the efferent arteriole, compounding the ACE inhibitor's effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: NSAIDs directly block renal potassium excretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: NSAIDs increase renin secretion from the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: NSAIDs sharply increase circulating angiotensin II levels

explanation.summary: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole while ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent, together dropping GFR.
explanation.whyCorrect: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins that normally dilate the afferent arteriole, reducing inflow. Coupled with efferent dilation from the ACE inhibitor, glomerular filtration pressure falls markedly, greatly increasing the risk of acute kidney injury. The brick lists this as a key drug interaction to avoid.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole by blocking prostaglandins; they do not dilate the efferent arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The shared risk here is reduced GFR and AKI, not a direct effect on potassium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased renin is not the mechanism; reduced afferent dilation is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The risk stems from altered renal blood flow, not a surge in angiotensin II.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old African American man develops swelling of the lips and tongue several hours after taking his first dose of an ACE inhibitor. Which of the following is the most feared complication of this reaction?

explanation.summary: Angioedema from ACE inhibitors is dangerous because it can obstruct the airway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased bradykinin can trigger angioedema, causing swelling of the face, lips, tongue, and upper airway. Airway obstruction is the most feared complication and can be fatal. African American patients have about a 4.5-fold greater risk of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute kidney injury is a hemodynamic effect unrelated to airway swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperkalemia is a separate metabolic adverse effect, not the danger of angioedema swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dry cough is a common, non-life-threatening bradykinin effect, not the feared angioedema complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rebound hypertension is not the described complication of angioedema.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with chronic hypertension who is 10 weeks pregnant asks whether her blood pressure medication is safe to continue. Which of the following antihypertensive classes is contraindicated because it is teratogenic and can cause fetal kidney injury?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists pregnancy as a contraindication to ACE inhibitors and ARBs because they are teratogenic and can cause fetal kidney injury. These agents should be stopped in a patient who is or may become pregnant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-methyldopa is not an ACE inhibitor and is not the class contraindicated for teratogenicity here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-blockers are not the class flagged in the brick as teratogenic RAAS inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium channel blockers are not identified as the pregnancy-contraindicated class here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiazide diuretics are not the teratogenic class discussed in this brick.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with known bilateral renal artery stenosis is being evaluated for blood pressure management. Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced renal blood flow makes the kidneys dependent on efferent constriction

choices.label: B
choices.text: They cause an excessive rise in circulating angiotensin II and aldosterone

choices.label: C
choices.text: They cause hyperkalemia by a mechanism independent of renal potassium handling

choices.label: D
choices.text: They increase urinary protein loss and worsen the degree of stenosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: They provoke reflex tachycardia that worsens renal perfusion pressure

explanation.summary: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, kidneys rely on efferent constriction to maintain filtration.
explanation.whyCorrect: With bilateral renal artery stenosis, renal blood flow is already low, and the kidneys depend on angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction to maintain glomerular pressure. ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove that tone, risking a decline in renal function, so they are contraindicated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These drugs lower or block angiotensin II activity; they do not raise it excessively.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperkalemia is a separate concern; the contraindication in stenosis is about renal perfusion and filtration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In stenosis the concern is falling GFR from loss of efferent tone, not increased proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reflex tachycardia is not the reason cited in the brick for this contraindication.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with diabetic chronic kidney disease is found to have proteinuria on urinalysis. Which medication class is first-line to reduce his proteinuria and slow progression of his renal disease?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line to reduce proteinuria in CKD.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic kidney disease with proteinuria, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line. By dilating the efferent arteriole they lower glomerular hydrostatic pressure, decreasing microalbuminuria and slowing progression of renal disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-blockers are used for cardiac indications and do not specifically reduce proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium channel blockers control blood pressure but are not first-line for proteinuria here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loop diuretics manage fluid balance but do not specifically reduce proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Statins lower cholesterol and do not directly reduce proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is started on an ACE inhibitor in addition to a beta-blocker and a loop diuretic. Beyond lowering blood pressure, what long-term benefit do ACE inhibitors provide in heart failure?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing heart rate to improve cardiac output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promoting sodium and water retention to raise preload

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raising serum potassium to protect the myocardium

explanation.summary: In heart failure, ACE inhibitors prevent maladaptive cardiac fibrosis and remodeling.
explanation.whyCorrect: By reducing angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors prevent the ventricular fibrosis and abnormal cardiac remodeling that angiotensin II promotes. This is why they are first-line in heart failure alongside beta-blockers and loop diuretics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE inhibitors reduce afterload; they do not increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors do not act by increasing heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They reduce sodium and water retention by lowering aldosterone, not promote it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising potassium is an adverse effect, not a therapeutic benefit.

questions.stem: A physician considers adding an ARB to a patient already taking an ACE inhibitor in an effort to improve blood pressure control. Why is combining these two classes generally avoided?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ARBs neutralize the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors

choices.label: B
choices.text: The combination causes severe reflex tachycardia

choices.label: C
choices.text: The combination increases the risk of hyperkalemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: The combination markedly increases the incidence of dry cough

choices.label: E
choices.text: They chemically inactivate one another in the bloodstream

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined because risks rise with no added benefit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used together because of additive adverse effects, including hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, and an increased risk of angioedema, while the combination has not been shown to provide additional clinical benefit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ARBs do not neutralize ACE inhibitors; both lower blood pressure by acting on the same pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reflex tachycardia is not the reason the combination is avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased cough is not the cited reason; the concern is hyperkalemia, AKI, and angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drugs do not chemically inactivate each other; the concern is additive physiologic toxicity.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on metformin. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which this drug lowers his blood glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased hepatic glucose production and improved peripheral insulin sensitivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of alpha-glucosidase enzymes in the intestinal brush border

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowing of gastric emptying and suppression of glucagon secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of glucose-independent insulin release from pancreatic beta cells

explanation.summary: Metformin, a biguanide, works mainly by lowering hepatic glucose output and increasing cellular sensitivity to insulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metformin acts primarily in the liver, skeletal muscle, and intestine. It decreases hepatic glucose production by reducing gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, decreases intestinal glucose absorption, and improves insulin sensitivity by increasing peripheral glucose uptake in skeletal muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking proximal tubule glucose reabsorption is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-glucosidase inhibition is a separate class not covered by metformin's action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slowing gastric emptying and lowering glucagon describes GLP-1 receptor agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin does not directly trigger insulin secretion; sulfonylureas cause glucose-independent insulin release.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A researcher studies how metformin increases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. Activation of which of the following proteins is chiefly responsible for triggering translocation of GLUT-4 to the cell membrane in these cells?

explanation.summary: Metformin stimulates AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that promotes GLUT-4 translocation in muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In skeletal muscle, metformin enhances glucose uptake and utilization by stimulating AMPK, the protein that monitors the ratio of AMP to ATP and ADP to ATP. Activated AMPK promotes GLUT-4 translocation to the cell membrane, moving glucose into muscle and fat cells in response to insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenylyl cyclase governs cAMP signaling and is not the protein metformin activates to move GLUT-4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DPP-4 degrades incretins and is unrelated to metformin's AMPK-driven action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The GLP-1 receptor mediates incretin signaling on pancreatic cells, not GLUT-4 translocation in muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SGLT2 is the renal transporter targeted by SGLT2 inhibitors, not the mediator of muscle glucose uptake.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes and obesity remains above her A1c goal on metformin. Her clinician wants to add an agent that can improve glucose control and promote weight loss with low risk of hypoglycemia when not combined with insulin or sulfonylureas. Which mechanism best describes this add-on therapy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking SGLT2 in the proximal tubule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists promote weight loss and glucose-dependent insulin secretion with low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLP-1 receptor agonists mimic the incretin GLP-1, binding GLP-1 receptors to increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, decrease glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and increase satiety, which reduces food intake and promotes weight loss. Because insulin release is glucose-dependent, hypoglycemia risk is low unless combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT2 blockade causes weight loss but does not act through incretin signaling or satiety.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Closing beta-cell KATP channels is the sulfonylurea mechanism and causes glucose-independent insulin release with weight gain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Replacing endogenous insulin describes insulin therapy, which promotes weight gain and hypoglycemia risk.
